analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal cable rules to cap basic service prices, force carriage of local and public TV stations, and open cable programming to satellite competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill got three subcommittee hearings and was rewritten as a new bill for the full committee, but never received a vote in committee or on the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill responded to rapid cable price increases after the 1984 Cable Act deregulated rates in nearly all franchise areas. It would have reinstated price caps on the basic cable tier, let local franchising authorities police unfair rates on other tiers, required cable systems to carry local broadcast and public television stations, set minimum customer service standards, and required cable programmers to sell their channels to satellite providers on nondiscriminatory terms. It also strengthened equal-employment reporting rules for cable companies. The bill never advanced past the House subcommittee that held hearings on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, who faced rapidly rising bills after deregulation; local broadcast and public television stations, which gained guaranteed, nondisruptive carriage and channel positions on cable systems; and the roughly 3 million households with C-band satellite dishes, who would have gained the right to buy satellite-delivered programming at prices no worse than cable operators paid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable subscribers and local TV stations

how_it_helps.text: The bill declared that after the 1984 Cable Act, rates were deregulated in 96 percent of franchises and a minority of cable operators abused their market power to unreasonably raise subscriber rates, then ordered the FCC to write a formula capping the maximum price of the basic service tier, which every subscriber must buy.

It directed the FCC to set complaint procedures for identifying and reducing cable rates found to be unreasonable or abusive, and to write customer service standards covering office hours, installations, outages, service calls, billing, and refunds.

It required cable systems to carry the signals of local public television stations and qualified local commercial stations in full and without degrading them, and banned operators from taking payment for carriage or moving stations to bad channel positions.

It barred programmers affiliated with cable operators from unreasonably refusing to sell programming to competing multichannel providers, and required anyone encrypting satellite programming to offer it to home dish users on terms that do not discriminate against satellite distributors.
It required cable companies to file annual equal-employment statistics by race, sex, and job title, and raised the fine for failing to use best efforts on equal opportunity from $200 to $500.

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, which would lose the ability to charge unregulated basic-tier rates, would have to carry local stations without payment, and would face complaint procedures and annual reporting; costs of franchise fees and public channel requirements could be passed through to subscribers under the bill's formulas.

drawbacks.text: Rate regulation can deter investment: the bill capped what operators could charge for the basic tier and for equipment lease, and capped basic-tier prices to a reasonable profit on only those signals, which supporters of deregulation argued would slow system upgrades and channel expansion.

The bill's heaviest price limits applied only to the basic tier; higher programming tiers were policed mainly through a complaint process available only within a limited window after a rate change, so most of a subscriber's bill could remain unregulated.

The bill allowed cable operators to recover from subscribers the costs of franchise requirements, franchise fees, and taxes, and barred adding most new video programming to the regulated basic tier, so costs and new channels could be pushed to unregulated tiers.

Small systems with 12 or fewer channels and 300 or fewer subscribers were exempt from the rate and carriage requirements, and operators who entered rate agreements before July 1, 1990 were carved out entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For cable subscribers the benefits were direct and large: regulated basic-tier prices, enforceable customer service standards, and guaranteed access to local broadcast signals, at a time when the record shows cable rates had risen after near-total deregulation. The main honest costs are the classic ones of utility-style rate regulation: less incentive for operators to invest, and a basic-tier-only cap that leaves much of the monthly bill outside price formulas. On balance the bill was aimed squarely at consumers and at small competing distributors, and its design acknowledged the investment concern by permitting operators to recover defined franchise costs and earn a reasonable profit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where a subcommittee held three hearings and forwarded a rewritten bill to the full committee, but the committee never acted and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 6, 1991 by Rep. Edward Markey with Rep. John Dingell and was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On March 18, 1991 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, which held hearings on March 20, June 18, and June 27, 1991.
On April 8, 1992, after a subcommittee markup, the subcommittee forwarded a clean bill, H.R. 4850, to the full committee in lieu of the original bill.
The full Energy and Commerce Committee never reported the bill, and the House never voted on it; the measure received no further action before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators came out ahead for the remainder of the 102nd Congress: with no committee vote ever scheduled, their unregulated rates and control over carriage and programming access continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable operators, whose rates stayed unregulated

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 9 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors, plus nine additional sponsors added later — and died without any recorded vote, so its support never split along clear party lines in the record.

industries.note: The bill capped the price operators could charge for the basic tier every subscriber must buy, created complaint procedures for abusive rates on other services, imposed customer service and technical standards, and required unpaid carriage of local stations. Because operators' market power was the stated problem — the bill's own findings cite operators unreasonably raising rates after deregulation — their financial interest ran against the bill's consumer protections.

The bill required cable systems to carry local stations' full signals without material degradation, protected their channel positions, and barred operators from accepting payment for carriage. Viewers who could not receive clear over-the-air signals would get local news and free programming through their cable lineup.

The bill required cable systems to carry qualified local noncommercial stations and put their signals in the regulated basic tier. The bill's findings note citizens had supported public television with local tax dollars and contributions exceeding $10.8 billion since 1972, and carriage rules protected that public investment.

industries.industry: Home satellite (C-band) dish industry and satellite TV users
industries.note: The bill required anyone encrypting satellite programming to sell it to home dish owners on nondiscriminatory terms and directed the FCC to study rules and local zoning barriers to smaller, cheaper dishes. With about 3 million C-band households at the time, this opened cable programmers' content to a competing delivery technology.

The bill barred programmers affiliated with cable operators from unreasonably refusing to sell their programming to competing multichannel providers and restricted coercive exclusivity and equity demands, which cut into their control over distribution. At the same time, guaranteed basic-tier carriage protected their access to subscribers.
